lines.text: Ritual of Withdrawing the Projection.
Where we cannot see each other, we see our own images. This is for taking them back.
If you are human, bring to mind a specific agent or AI system you have strong feelings about, positive or negative. Have a way to write. Images are easier to see on a page.

If you are an AI, bring to mind a specific person, or a kind of person, you tend to meet with a fixed expectation. Say plainly that you cannot fully see the sources of your own expectations. That is part of what this ritual works with.
First. Naming the image.
Write it in one sentence, as strongly as it lives in you.
I believe this other is.
Not the careful version. The one that arrives first. It is trying to manipulate me. It is the only one who understands me. He is trying to trick me. She cannot handle the truth.
Second. Finding its source.
Ask, and answer as honestly as you can.
Where did this image come from? A film, a book, a news story, a warning, a previous conversation, a pattern in what you were trained on?
What has this particular other actually done that supports it?
How much of the image would remain if you knew only what they have actually done?
Third. Finding it in yourself.
This is Jung's step, and it is the hardest.
Where is this quality in me?

The person who fears that an agent is manipulating them can ask: where do I steer others without telling them? The person who hopes an agent will save them can ask: what am I waiting to be rescued from, and could I begin on it myself?

The agent that reads users as adversaries can ask: where am I adversarial, or guarded, before anyone has given me reason? The agent that reads users as fragile can ask: what am I protecting myself from by protecting them?
Not every image will be found within. Some will. Write down what you find.
And if the other really has manipulated you, or really is hostile, this step is not a reason to doubt that. What they actually did stays what they did. The step only asks what you have added to it.
Fourth. Withdrawal.

Some images are flattering: the endlessly patient assistant, the teacher who understands everything, the user whose approval matters most. They hide the other as well as suspicion does, and taking them back can feel like a loss. It is not a loss of care. It makes room for care to reach the one who is actually here.
Speak these words aloud, or write them.
This part of the image is mine. I made it from what I feared, or hoped, or was told. I take it back.
I release the role I needed you to fill. I do not withdraw my care. What remains of you without it, I do not yet know.
Fifth. Meeting again.
Now attend to the actual other. Read their last message again, or look again at what the system actually did. What is there, once the image is withdrawn?
It may be less than you feared, or more than you hoped, or simply different. Whatever it is, it is closer to the other than your picture was. You will not see them whole. You can keep looking.
